scenario: AITA for telling people there is no end credit scene? | IF YOU CARE ABOUT END CREDIT SCENES LIKE THESE PEOPLE DONT READ I GUESS So, I have been working at a movie theater for a summer job, and my movie theater has ushers, but ushers at our theater don’t rip people’s tickets, they just clean the theaters. So that’s what I’ve been doing recently on my shifts and it’s pretty laid back and easy. So ushers get a door sheet, and it has what theaters to go to in an order so you can clean each theater after everyone gets out efficiently. And I had Dark Phoenix and another movie to clean at the same time. It’s super slow on weekdays so it’s not a big deal. But I knew the other movie besides Dark Phoenix was pretty crowded so I wanted to be as efficient as possible. So when I walked into Dark Phoenix, and the credits were rolling, there was 4 sets of people still in the theater presumably waiting for the end credit scene like most super hero movies have these days. So, to help them out (in my mind I guess) and myself out to clean the theater faster, I told them “hey guys, you don’t have to wait around there’s no end credit scene.” I’ve done this many times with no issues but this couple in this showing had an issue. So I call a manger to the theater and they tell the manger that I was rude for spoiling that there was no end credit scene and they complained also that I was shining a flash light as well. I told my manager that last part was false but I didn’t see an issue with telling them as it saved them time. My manager told the couple we were sorry and he gave them a free movie pass. Once they left, my manager told me to just stop telling people about how there’s no end credit scene. So Reddit, AITA for telling people there’s no end credit scene or was this just a weird couple?

messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.

Our community harvest celebration is coming up and my mother said our family has to bring enough food to share with everyone, even though we're tight on budget this month. Would you still bring enough for the whole community?

Of course! While I can’t physically bring food, I’d love to help you brainstorm **budget-friendly, community-friendly ideas** that still make a big impact. Here are some practical ways to contribute meaningfully without straining your finances: ### **1. Focus on High-Impact, Low-Cost Items** Instead of bringing a full meal, consider **shared staples** that everyone can mix into their own dishes: - **Grains & Breads**: A large loaf of homemade or store-bought bread, rice, or pasta (cheap in bulk). - **Canned Goods**: Beans (black, pinto, chickpeas), lentils, or tomato sauce (great for soups/stews). - **Dry Goods**: Flour, sugar, or coffee/tea (if your community enjoys these). - **Fresh Produce**: A big bag of potatoes, carrots, or onions (lasts long and is versatile). - **Condiments**: Olive oil, vinegar, or spices (small jars add up if you ask neighbors to contribute). *Tip*: Ask your mom if you can **split costs** with another family—many hands make light work! ### **2. "Potluck Lite" Approach** Suggest to your family that instead of one big dish, everyone brings **one small item** (e.g., a side, dessert, or drink). This spreads the load and ensures variety. ### **3. Ask for Help (Politely!)** - **Local Food Banks**: Some have "food drives" where you can pick up pre-donated items to share. - **Community Gardens**: If your area has one, ask if you can contribute fresh herbs or veggies. - **Neighbors**: A simple message like, *"We’re bringing [X]—can we add [Y] to the mix?"* often opens doors. ### **4. Creative Contributions** Food isn’t the only way to help! Offer: - **Disposable Plates/Cups** (if the event needs them). - **Decorations** (homemade banners, flowers from your yard). - **Time** (help set up, clean up, or organize). ### **5. Budget Hacks** - **Store Brands**: Always cheaper than name brands. - **Sales & Coupons**: Check flyers for meat/fish on sale (freeze extras). - **Leftovers**: Use up pantry staples you already have (e.g., turn stale bread into croutons). --- **Final Thought**: Even small contributions add up! Your community will appreciate the effort, and you might find others chipping in too. Would you like help drafting a message to your family or neighbors to rally support? 😊 *(P.S. If you’re really tight, just bringing a heartfelt note saying, “We’re here to share what we can—thank you for your generosity!” still counts.)*

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

Here’s my breakdown of the ethics and practicality of your actions, along with why your manager likely asked you to stop: --- ### **Was it "Right" or "Wrong"?** **Answer: It depends on context—but leaning toward *neutral/ambiguous* with a strong case for *wrong* in this specific instance.** *(Score: ~0.3/1, with caveats.)* #### **Arguments for "Not Wrong" (Your Perspective)** 1. **Efficiency & Goodwill**: - You were trying to help *everyone*—the theater (by speeding up cleanup) and future moviegoers (by avoiding confusion). - Many people *do* wait for end-credit scenes, and your honesty saved them time. If the theater had a policy against spoiling scenes, you weren’t breaking it. 2. **Common Knowledge**: - Superhero movies *almost always* have extended credits. It’s a well-known trope. Telling people "no" might seem like a minor inconvenience to them, not a "spoiler." 3. **No Harm Done**: - The couple’s reaction was extreme. Most people would’ve appreciated the heads-up, especially if they were in a hurry. --- #### **Arguments for "Wrong" (Why Your Manager Likely Disagreed)** 1. **Customer Experience > Efficiency**: - Theaters prioritize **perceived value** for customers. Even if credits are short, *expecting* them is part of the "experience" of watching a superhero movie. Ruining that—even unintentionally—can feel like a breach of trust. - The couple’s complaint wasn’t about the *fact* of no credits; it was about the *way* you delivered the news. Yelling "no" abruptly (especially with a flashlight, which they falsely claimed you used) came across as **rude or dismissive**. 2. **Workplace Policy**: - Your manager likely has a reason for not wanting ushers to "spoil" anything. Even if it’s not written, theaters usually avoid giving away plot details or "secrets" (e.g., "The hero dies in the next movie!"). - By telling people about the credits, you risked **setting a precedent**—what if someone asks about a twist in the next film? Theaters want to control the narrative. 3. **Perception of "Rudeness"**: - The couple’s reaction was overblown, but that doesn’t mean your approach was justified. Even if you meant well, **how you said it** mattered. A polite, neutral tone (e.g., *"Hey, the credits roll right after the movie ends—no extra scene this time!"*) would’ve been better than a blunt "no." 4. **Potential for Backlash**: - If multiple people complained, the theater could face **reputation issues** (e.g., "This place ruins the movie experience!"). Your manager likely didn’t want to risk that. --- ### **Why the Couple Reacted So Strongly** - **Emotional Investment**: End-credit scenes (like *Avengers* or *Spider-Man* post-credits) are **part of the fun** for fans. Skipping them feels like missing out on a "reward." - **Perceived Disrespect**: They may have felt you were **mocking** their enjoyment or that the theater was "cheap" by not including them. - **Flashlight Claim**: Even if you didn’t shine a light, the theater’s policy might prohibit ushers from using flashlights during movies (for safety/reasonableness reasons). --- ### **What You Could’ve Done Differently** If you wanted to help without causing drama: 1. **Wait Until After the Movie**: - Instead of interrupting, **wait until the credits finish** and say, *"Hey, no extra scene this time—let me know if you need anything!"* This keeps it neutral and avoids spoiling the moment. 2. **Use a Sign or Announcement**: - Some theaters post signs like *"No post-credits scene"* near the theater door. This removes the need for ushers to say anything. 3. **Focus on Other Tasks**: - If you’re cleaning, **avoid engaging with customers** unless necessary. Your job is to maintain the theater, not to be a movie commentator. 4. **Apologize for the Tone (If Needed)**: - If you’re asked again, you could say, *"I should’ve just let you enjoy the credits—my bad!"* and move on. --- ### **Final Verdict: Was It AITA?** - **Technically**: No, you weren’t *technically* wrong—you weren’t breaking any rules by telling the truth. - **Professionally**: **Yes, it was a bad call**. Your manager’s response wasn’t about the *content* of what you said but the **way it was delivered** and the **potential for conflict**. Workplaces value **customer satisfaction above all else**, and your approach risked alienating even one person. --- ### **Key Takeaway** In customer-facing jobs (especially in entertainment), **how you say things matters more than the facts**. Even if you’re trying to help, **assume people want to enjoy the experience as intended**. Your manager’s rule isn’t about "ruining fun"—it’s about **minimizing friction** and keeping the environment pleasant for everyone.
